data:
Socrates Montis (born Socrates Monastriotis) was born on August 15, 1897, in the village of Kerkyra, located in Corfu then under Ottoman rule. His early years were shaped by the turbulence of the Greco-Turkish War of 1897, a brief but deeply symbolic conflict in which Greece attempted to assert its sovereignty over Ottoman-held territories. Though the war ended in defeat for Greece, it stirred nationalist and democratic ideals in many young Greeks, ideas that would resonate with Montis throughout his life.

His father, George Montis, was a minor government clerk, while his mother, Vasiliky Liopoulou, came from a family of tradespeople, likely living off the land. Socrates received a limited formal education, typical for many rural Greeks, but grew up steeped in both the oral traditions of his village and the nationalist sentiment circulating in the waning years of Ottoman rule. After the Balkan Wars of 1912–13 further destabilized the region and redefined borders across southeastern Europe, the Monastriotis family joined the broader wave of Greek migration to America. At 17, Socrates disembarked at Ellis Island in 1914 and adopted the simplified surname “Montis,” as many immigrants did to assimilate more easily while preserving a connection to their heritage.

In New York City, Montis settled in the growing Greek community of Astoria, Queens. Like many Greek immigrants of the time, he found work in the food service industry, likely first as a dishwasher, then as a waiter in the cafeterias and hotel kitchens of Lower Manhattan. There, his political consciousness began to sharpen. Witnessing long hours, poor wages, and exploitative conditions, Montis joined Local 16 of the American Federation of Labor (AFL), a food workers union increasingly influenced by leftist organizers. He became an active participant in organized labor actions, attending rallies, distributing pamphlets, and forming bonds with fellow immigrant workers: Italians, Jews, Irish, who like him, dreamed of a fairer and more dignified life.

By the mid-1930s, fascism was spreading across Europe. Montis grew increasingly alarmed by reports of Mussolini in Italy and Hitler in Germany. In 1936, the Spanish Civil War broke out after General Francisco Franco led a military coup against Spain’s democratically elected Popular Front government. When Montis heard from fellow unionists that the Communist Party and other left-wing groups were recruiting international volunteers to fight for the Spanish Republic, he felt called. Despite having no military experience, he volunteered.

In January 1937, at the age of 40 (the older end for international volunteers), Montis sailed aboard the SS Paris to France, falsely claiming to be a philosophy student, his Greek name lending credibility to the cover story. He crossed the Pyrenees on foot, evading customs officials and border guards, and entered Spain illegally, made necessary by the U.S. Neutrality Acts, which forbade American citizens from participating in foreign wars. Upon arrival in Spain, he was assigned to the Abraham Lincoln Battalion, a unit of the XV International Brigade composed largely of American volunteers.

Training was brief and chaotic, conducted mostly in French and Spanish neither of which Montis could have understood well. Still, his resolve was unshaken. His first and only engagement came at the Battle of Jarama in February 1937, a brutal and chaotic confrontation near Madrid meant to halt Franco’s advance and prevent the capital from being surrounded. The battalion suffered heavy casualties, and Montis was gravely wounded during the fighting. He was evacuated to Madrid, and later to a hospital in Barcelona, where despite efforts to save him, he died from his injuries in March 1937.
News of Montis’s death and his fellow comrades reached back to New York. For his comrades, he became a symbol of international solidarity and working-class courage. Though omitted from official histories during the Cold War and the McCarthy era, Montis’s name lives on in the archives of the Abraham Lincoln Brigade, alongside hundreds of other volunteers who crossed oceans and borders to defend democracy. He remains one of the many unsung heroes of the twentieth century: an immigrant, a worker, and, in his final days, a soldier for a freer world.
